title: NVIDIA: Data Centers Aren't Cost Centers—They're Token Factories
dek: Moore's Law's physical dividend ended long ago; NVIDIA pursues ‘extreme co-design’ across five layers—energy, chips, infrastructure, models, apps—to aggressively boost tokens per watt and per dollar.
why: Dense technical detail (liquid cooling, copper-cable limits, optical interconnect, agent-memory architecture) for those wanting to understand the bottom-layer engineering logic of AI factories; limited signal for readers focused only on business narrative.
who: Engineers tracking AI infrastructure engineering details, data center and cloud computing procurement decision-makers, and investors wanting to understand why NVIDIA calls itself an infrastructure company rather than purely a chip company.

points.h: Data Centers Shift from Cost Centers to Token-Printing Revenue Engines
points.body: The keynote opened by clarifying the paradigm shift: data centers previously ran IT applications and were pure cost centers; AI factories must generate tokens efficiently to create revenue. This positioning shift is the starting point for all subsequent engineering decisions—energy, chips, cooling—and every optimization targets raising tokens per dollar and per watt.

points.h: Moore's Law's Physical Promise Broke Two Decades Ago
points.body: Transistor counts do keep doubling, but Moore's Law originally included a physical and economic promise of doubling at the same power and cost—this part stopped working after Dennard scaling ended around 2005. This is the fundamental reason NVIDIA bet on accelerated computing and rewrote single-threaded applications as GPU-parallel applications, not mere marketing narrative.

points.h: Mixture-of-Experts Models Triggered Token Consumption Jump
points.body: Model parameter scaling at roughly 10x annually is a stable trend, but Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models a year and a half ago created an inflection point: models began ‘reasoning’ and generating one output token internally creates up to 100x more tokens. The arrival of agents will accelerate this demand further, which is why NVIDIA must continuously drive down cost per token.

points.h: Energy Storage Flattens AI Training's Power Spikes
points.body: During AI training, thousands of GPUs synchronize collective communications like a giant computer, and power load swings wildly like a downpour, damaging supply transformers. NVIDIA uses energy-storage systems like DSX Flex/DSX LPS to store excess power and release it during peak demand, flattening the consumption curve. This single optimization enables 40% more GPU deployment from the same 1 gigawatt power, directly translating to 40% more revenue.

points.h: Inference Complexity Demands Multi-Chip System Design
points.body: Industry once assumed inference would be simpler than training, but MoE models impose heavy demands on both NVLink vertical scaling and cross-rack horizontal scaling, and agent workloads raise stakes further. NVIDIA's answer couples Rubin GPU and Vera CPU tightly via high-performance, cache-coherent chip-to-chip interconnect, then scales within cabinets via NVLink and across data centers via Spectrum-6, claiming this delivers 10x token throughput and one-tenth the per-token cost.

points.h: Copper Signal Degradation Drives Optical Interconnect Adoption
points.body: To save power, NVIDIA insists ‘use copper when you can’, but high-speed signals travel only meters over copper cables, so they cram GPUs into the same cabinet with liquid cooling. Counterintuitively, even within a rack, signals degrade crossing those short copper traces on PCB, requiring re-amplification and optical-module drive; co-packaged optics (CPO) switches solder optical transceivers directly beside the ASIC, eliminating that degradation and saving tens of megawatts in AI factories—power saved becomes tokens generated.

points.h: Agents Loop AI Output Back as Input, Bypassing Humans
points.body: Agents' essence is AI looping its output back as input, no longer relying on human prompts—humans are too slow, AI too fast and too ‘impatient’, creating AI-to-AI dialogue chains. Vera CPU is built specifically to run these agent toolchains: planning, coding, summarizing and compressing results, directly raising demands on memory and interconnect bandwidth—from 800G to 1600G/second.

points.h: Agent Memory Architecture Demands Dual-Layer Storage Design
points.body: NVIDIA analogizes KV cache as agent short-term memory, files and objects and vector databases as long-term memory, and designed CMX (short-term) and STX (long-term) reference architectures accordingly. This new architecture reportedly delivers 5x token throughput and 5x efficiency—storage no longer merely stores data but directly determines agent ‘thinking’ speed.

terms.def: Simultaneous cross-layer optimization across five layers—energy, chips, infrastructure, models, apps—rather than optimizing any single layer alone.
Packages optical transceivers directly beside the switch chip, reducing signal loss and power consumption on PCB copper traces.
Intermediate state saved after a large language model processes text, equivalent to an agent's ‘short-term memory’.
Architecture that dynamically invokes partial ‘expert’ sub-networks during model inference, significantly increasing internal token consumption.
NVIDIA's high-bandwidth interconnect technology between GPUs within a cabinet, enabling multiple GPUs to run cooperatively as one computer.

As a result of all of this, with the excess, we can deploy 40% more GPUs in an AI factory, per gigawatt of power. 40% more GPUs means 40% more tokens and 40% more revenues.
This extreme co-design delivers 10x more tokens and one-tenth the cost per token by optimizing across this stack. Everybody said that inferencing was going to be easy. It's incredibly complicated.
So we have to reproduce the electrical signal and make it beautiful again, and then we drive the optics.
An agent is AI eating its own tail. Instead of humans generating prompts, AI closes the loop and feeds the prompt back to itself.
